newsitem.title: CHILE: Foreign investment in Latam rises steeply - U.N.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investment in Latam rises steeply - U.N.

text.p: Foreign investment in Latin America is likely to rise to $37 billion this year with privatizations and oil and mining projects topping investors' shopping list, said a United Nations expert Tuesday.

"Last year, our expectations were more than fulfilled and conditions are favorable for very strong growth in 1997," said Patricio Rozas, an economist at the U.N. Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLA), which is based in Santiago. "But much will depend on what happens in the Mexican and Brazilian economies."
ECLA estimated foreign investment reached $30 billion in last year, up from nearly $24 billion in 1995 and just $8 billion at the start of the decade.
The rise reflects the internationalization of the region's economies, as well as recovery from the turmoil of the debt crises that plagued Latin America in the 1980s, he said.

"The increase is the result of political stability and sustained economic growth since 1990," Rozas told a news conference to present ECLA's report on foreign investment in the region in 1995. "The 1980s were a completely lost decade for Latin America."
Projects that have attracted a flood of international capital include state telecom sale in Brazil and Peru, mining projects in Chile and plans to improve infrastructure in Argentina.
Brazil attracted $6.3 billion worth of foreign investment in the first five months of the year, while investment in Venezuela amounted to a huge $2 billion in May alone.
"Venezuela has been on the sidelines for a long time, but this year we have seen a spectacular recovery," he said.
Despite the increase, foreign investment only totals around seven percent of total investment in Latin America with most projects financed by local capital, he said.

Direct foreign investment in most countries in the region rose in 1995, despite the financial crisis sparked by Mexico's shock devaluation in late 1994. But in Mexico, investment plunged nearly 40 percent to $7 billion from $11 billion in 1994.
